canonical_title: Schizophrenia and the Book of Changes
author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Dick's essay linking schizophrenia, the experience of time, and the I Ching, arguing that the schizophrenic and the oracle both collapse ordinary sequence into a single, acausal present.
page_summary:
In this essay Dick brings together three of his lifelong preoccupations, mental illness, the structure of time, and the Chinese Book of Changes, and treats them as facets of a single problem. He proposes that the schizophrenic does not so much lose reality as fall out of ordinary temporal sequence, experiencing past, present, and future as a simultaneous, undifferentiated now rather than as a causal chain.

Dick connects this altered time-sense to the I Ching, the oracle he consulted while composing The Man in the High Castle. The hexagram, he suggests, works by the same acausal logic Jung called synchronicity: it reads the total configuration of a moment rather than tracing cause to effect. In this light the schizophrenic and the diviner occupy neighboring positions, both perceiving pattern where linear consciousness perceives only succession.

The essay is an early and important statement of Dick's conviction that psychosis and mystical perception may share a common architecture, a theme he would pursue at length in the Exegesis.
